source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving (book), as described by Li et al. 2025
finding: Schoenfeld framed problem solving as a time-ordered chain of episodes: Read, Analyze, Explore, Plan, Implement, Verify. The theory separates what a solver knows from how it deploys that knowledge. Expert skill rests on control (planning, monitoring, evaluating), not on more domain facts. Monitor was added later as a seventh label for brief metacognitive moves.
numbers: Built on hundreds of hours of videotaped think-aloud sessions of students on non-routine problems (per Li et al.).
quote: expert performance hinges less on sheer domain knowledge than on the dynamic orchestration of planning, monitoring, and evaluation
limits: Second-hand. I could not open the book or the 1981 and 1992 chapters. Original episode counts, timeline-graph numbers and the share of attempts with no control were not verified.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for a coded episode log. Control as the key variable matches our rule that code, not the model, decides transitions.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (search-result summaries only)
finding: Summaries say novices hurry to an answer, apply procedures without checking them, and wander into wild goose chases. Control skill keeps resources from being wasted. General heuristics such as means-ends analysis were reported as nearly useless in content-rich maths domains.
numbers: No figures verified. The often-quoted share of student attempts that pick a path and never monitor it could not be confirmed this session.
limits: Secondary. The mathed.net page only cites the chapter and quotes a remark about executive or control skills. The scanned chapter PDF had no text layer. Do not cite a percentage from this line.
agent_relevance: The wild-goose-chase idea is the human ancestor of our impasse detector: commit, never evaluate, burn budget.

source: Artzt and Armour-Thomas (1992) Development of a cognitive-metacognitive framework for protocol analysis of mathematical problem solving in small groups
finding: Extended the episode scheme to small groups. Categories reported by later users: read, understand, explore, analyze, plan, implement, verify, watch and listen. Each segment is coded as cognitive or metacognitive.
numbers: Sample reported in an ERIC abstract: 27 seventh-grade students in small groups on one maths problem.
limits: Only search snippets seen, not the paper. Group setting, school-age children.
agent_relevance: The episode scheme was already adapted once with an extra Understand code. Our Read plus Analyze split may be enough; add no codes without a test.

source: Harskamp and Suhre (2007) Schoenfeld's problem solving theory in a student controlled learning environment
finding: Cited by both LLM papers as the human-research use of episode theory. Not opened.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: A source to open later if we need a human baseline for episode frequencies.

source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models: A Perspective from Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
finding: First application of Schoenfeld episodes to a reasoning model. Seven sentence labels (Read, Analyze, Plan, Implement, Explore, Verify, Monitor) plus three paragraph labels (General, Explore, Verify). The corpus and guidebooks are public: DeepSeek-R1 answers to SAT maths.
numbers: Items drawn from 1,385 SAT Math questions across 19 skills. Hand-annotated: 38 responses (2 per skill), 915 paragraphs, 3,087 sentences. Three trained annotators after a pilot where two authors each labelled 5 responses.
limits: One model, one moderate-difficulty exam. No inter-annotator kappa appears in the text I read. Authors list narrow scope and moderate automatic accuracy as limits. Correctness was not tested.
agent_relevance: Ready-made label set and guidebook we can reuse for logging our own traces.

source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models: A Perspective from Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
finding: Human-labelled sentence transitions in R1 traces are sticky and ordered like human solving. Largest off-diagonal moves: Read to Analyze, Plan to Implement, Explore to Analyze.
numbers: Row probabilities (Figure 1): Read to Read .34, Read to Analyze .29; Analyze to Analyze .54; Plan to Implement .40; Implement to Implement .63, Implement to Verify .18; Explore to Explore .34, Explore to Analyze .25, Explore to Verify .12, Explore to Monitor .10; Verify to Verify .51; Monitor to Read .20, Monitor to Analyze .21.
limits: Single model, 3,087 sentences. Descriptive only, not related to correctness in this paper. Column order in the extracted figure is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Baseline Markov profile. Explore self-loops far above .34 would be off the normal profile.

source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models: A Perspective from Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
finding: Prompting LLMs to auto-label sentences: the written guidebook helps most, examples help less. Best setting is GPT-4.1 with examples plus guidebook.
numbers: Sentence accuracy, base / example / guidebook / both. GPT-4.1 .595/.604/.676/.681. Gemini-2.0 .590/.628/.655/.626. GPT-4o .475/.504/.577/.609. GPT-4.1 paragraph accuracy rises from .444 to .757 with both. Run on all annotated data.
limits: Table 2 shows .681 for GPT-4.1 on all data. The 0.805 headline comes from a separate 30% test subset in Table 4.
agent_relevance: A written guidebook is worth more than examples. Same lesson for any judge prompt we write.

source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models: A Perspective from Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
finding: Headline labelling result. GPT-4.1 with examples and guidebook reaches 0.805 sentence accuracy (kappa 0.764) on a 30% test subset. A fine-tuned BERT gets 0.732.
numbers: Accuracy / kappa: GPT-4.1 .805/.764; BERT .732/.671; RoBERTa .730/.670; SVM on Gemini embeddings .704/.632; MLP .684/.613; KNN .587/.490. Training used a 70/30 split of the 38 responses.
quote: GPT-4.1 obtains the best results, with the highest accuracy (0.805) and the highest kappa (0.764).
limits: Test subset is about 30% of 3,087 sentences from only 38 responses, so the interval is wide. Compared with Table 2 the same model scores .681 on all data, so the headline is on a favourable split.
agent_relevance: A cheap fine-tuned BERT is within 0.07 of GPT-4.1. A live episode tagger need not call a large model.

source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models: A Perspective from Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
finding: Where even the best labeller fails: Analyze vs Verify and Implement vs Verify. Verify is the hard class to separate from neighbours.
numbers: GPT-4.1 confusion (percent of all sentences, true to predicted): Analyze to Verify 4.8, Analyze to Explore 2.3, Implement to Verify 3.2, Verify to Implement 0.3. Diagonal: Analyze 16.6, Implement 17.1, Verify 18.5, Explore 6.1, Monitor 5.2.
limits: Percentages are from the printed table.
agent_relevance: A detector that keys on Verify counts will be noisy. Use Explore and Monitor, or code checks, for the stuck signal.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Scales episode labelling to 15 models and adds an Answer label (8 labels). Sentence level only. GPT-5 is the annotator, picked from four candidates on a human gold set.
numbers: Corpus: 100 Omni-MATH problems x 15 models = 1,500 responses, 410,991 sentences. Gold set: 9 problems, 7,067 hand-labelled sentences. Overall accuracy / kappa: GPT-4.1 86.10/82.74, GPT-5 86.33/82.85, Gemini-2.5-Flash 82.90/78.67, Gemini-2.5-Pro 80.89/75.96. Non-reasoning traces are easier (GPT-5 89.34 accuracy) than reasoning traces (86.02).
limits: Labels come from an LLM, so labelling noise is a stated limit. Maths only. Agreement is with the authors' own gold set.
agent_relevance: Episode labels can be produced at about 86% agreement with humans on long traces. Good enough for diagnostics, not for hard decisions.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Episodes follow a time pattern the authors call a heartbeat. Early: Read, Analyze, Plan, Explore, falling. Middle: Implement peaks. Late: Verify rises and Monitor is U-shaped. Answer is near zero until the end.
numbers: Seen in five open reasoning models: DeepSeek-R1, Phi-4-Reasoning, Qwen-3-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, on traces normalised to 0 to 100 percent progress.
limits: Mean curves; individual traces vary. Olympiad problems only.
agent_relevance: A healthy trace has a shape. Explore still high late in the trace is an off-shape sign that code can test cheaply.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Reasoning models spend tokens very differently from instruction models. Non-reasoning models are Implement-heavy and almost never Explore or Verify. Distilled small models copy the teacher's episode mix.
limits: o1-mini and o3-mini were seen only through final answers, so they look like non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold can create the missing Explore and Verify share in a plain model, but G11 says to cap it.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Which short episode patterns separate reasoning traces from final answers and from non-reasoning output. Small Explore, Monitor and Verify loops are the signature of reasoning models.
numbers: Top mutual-information patterns, reasoning trace vs its own answer: Exp-Mon .2862, Ver-Exp .2815, Mon-Exp .2771, Exp-Plan .2754. Versus non-reasoning models: Exp-Mon .2510, Mon-Exp .2405, Exp-Ana-Imp .2073.
limits: Mutual information shows presence, not benefit.
agent_relevance: Explore-Monitor-Explore is normal for reasoning models. A coded detector needs length or repetition, not just the pattern.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Episode features predict answer correctness. Lasso logistic regression on global stats, 8 episode ratios and the 8x8 transition counts. Explore followed by Monitor or Analyze goes with correct answers. A high Explore share, Explore followed by Verify, and Explore followed by Answer go with wrong ones.
numbers: 500 stratified traces from 5 open models. Positive coefficients: Exp to Mon +0.41, Exp to Ana +0.31, Mon to Ana +0.28, Read to Ver +0.27, Ans to Ver +0.22, Ver ratio +0.21. Negative: Explore ratio -0.54, Exp to Ver -0.45, Exp to Ans -0.41, total count -0.36, Imp to Read -0.32, Imp to Imp -0.28.
quote: sustained exploration without subsequent stabilization is associated with incorrect outcomes
limits: Association from a sparse linear model on 500 traces. No held-out accuracy or AUC in the text I read. Problem difficulty is not controlled, and hard problems produce both more Explore and more errors. Not causal.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for a coded impasse detector. Candidate rule: a high share of Explore that never routes to Monitor or Analyze, or ends in Answer.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Efficient-reasoning methods remove different episodes. L1 and ThinkPrune cut Verify and Analyze and become Implement-heavy. Arora and Zanette keeps the baseline mix. L1 loses verification loops most.
numbers: Baseline R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: Verify 11.43%, 9,897 tokens. L1: Verify 6.99%, 2,437 tokens. ThinkPrune: Verify 8.37%, 4,054 tokens. A&Z: Verify 9.94%, 5,312 tokens. Largest lost pattern MI: L1 N-V-N .3762, ThinkPrune N-V-N .1506, A&Z top .1039.
limits: Accuracy of the efficient models is not reported in this section, so we cannot say which removals cost accuracy.
agent_relevance: Cutting length by deleting Verify may hurt. Our Verify state (S8) is run by code and can stay while Explore is capped.

source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025/2026) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: On easy problems (50 GSM8K items) non-reasoning models skip Explore and Verify almost entirely, while Qwen-3-32B in reasoning mode puts most tokens into Verify.
numbers: Qwen-3-32B reasoning: Verify 55.89%. DeepSeek-R1: Verify 8.19%, Explore 6.88%. Gemini-2.0-Flash: Explore 0.00, Verify 1.35, Implement 55.58. Non-thinking Qwen-3-32B: Explore 0.00, Verify 0.00.
limits: Only 4 models and 50 items. Heavy verification on easy items looks like overthinking, but accuracy is not shown.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and G12: verification budget should scale with difficulty.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Wandering in numbers. In wrong answers, o1-like models switch between thoughts more often than in right ones. Conventional models do not. Switching rises with difficulty. Wrong answers often contain an early thought that was right but dropped.
numbers: Test sets: MATH500 (Level 5 as Hard), GPQA Diamond (198 questions), AIME 2024 plus AIME 2022 and 2023 (90 items). Models: QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1-671B, R1-Preview. Over 70% of incorrect responses hold at least one correct thought. In over 50% of incorrect responses more than 10% of thoughts are correct. Example trace: 25 thoughts, 7,270 extra tokens after a correct first thought.
quote: models frequently switch between different reasoning thoughts without sufficiently exploring promising paths
limits: A thought is split at cue words like 'alternatively' by Llama-3.3-70B. A thought counts as correct if either of two R1-distilled models gives it confidence 2 of 2. That judge was checked on 90 final thoughts (35 correct, 55 incorrect): 82.9% and 81.8% accuracy.
agent_relevance: Concrete wild-goose-chase signal: many short thoughts, none deepened. Fits an impasse rule if depth per thought is tracked.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: The underthinking score UT is the share of tokens in a wrong answer that come after the first correct thought. Higher UT is more waste. A stronger model can have higher UT on some sets.
numbers: UT (lower is better) with accuracy on MATH500-Hard: QwQ-32B-Preview 84.3 acc / 58.2 UT; R1-Preview 83.6 / 61.5; R1-671B 92.5 / 65.4. On AIME2024, R1-671B has both higher accuracy and lower UT.
limits: UT needs a ground-truth answer and a thought judge, so it is an offline metric, not a live signal.
agent_relevance: Use to grade our own logs after a run, not to steer a run.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: A decoding fix, the thought-switching penalty (TIP), lowers logits of switch tokens for a window after each thought starts. It raises accuracy without fine-tuning. A prompt instruction alone barely moved it.
numbers: Pass@1 without and with TIP. AIME2024: QwQ 38.3 to 44.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1; R1 73.8 to 74.8 (R1 plus prompt: 72.4). MATH500-Hard QwQ 83.1 to 83.7. GPQA QwQ 57.6 to 59.1. Self-consistency Pass@4 for QwQ on AIME2024 43.7 to 51.4. R1-Distill-Qwen-32B UT 8.7 to 7.3 with laconic decoding plus TIP. Grid: strength 3 to 30, duration 300 to 700 tokens, tuned on AIME 2022-23.
limits: Tuned on AIME 2022-23 with QwQ then reused on other models. Gain on R1 is one point. Needs logit access, which an API agent lacks.
agent_relevance: Prompting to persist did nothing, so persistence must be enforced by code, for example a minimum number of steps in one plan before reframing.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Overthinking in the other direction: too many solutions on easy problems. The first solution is usually already correct and later solutions add little that is new.
numbers: For 2 plus 3, o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one example had 13 solutions. In over 92% of cases the first solution round was already correct, and the first round was usually under 60% of the response (287 tokens, 38.7%, on ASDIV for QwQ-32B-Preview). Outcome efficiency under 50% on Level 1 problems.
limits: ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME with QwQ-32B-Preview and similar. Efficiency metrics are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Supports stopping after the first checked pass on easy items (G11, G12).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Self-training on shortened traces cuts tokens without losing accuracy on easy sets. Keeping only the first correct solution hurts on hard items, and adding a second solution as reflection repairs most of that.
numbers: Token cut 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview at kept accuracy. SimPO alone cut tokens 22.3% on MATH500. First-correct plus reflection beat first-correct only by 1.4% on the hard MATH500 set. Training data PRM12K, 10 samples per item at temperature 1.0.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, so not usable by a scaffold directly. Solution 2 is often a re-check with the same strategy.
agent_relevance: One extra independent check after the first correct answer is the sweet spot. Matches our single Verify state with an independent test.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) LCoT2Tree: structural patterns of long chain-of-thought predict correctness
finding: Turning a long chain into a tree (branch on thought switches, backtrack to earlier steps) predicts correctness better than length. Length alone is a weak signal.
numbers: Five models (DeepSeek-32B, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B, Seed-1.5-Thinking-pro, Grok-3-mini) on MATH Level 5, GPQA, LiveCodeBench, MMLU-Pro. Length-only classifier: 60.0% on MMLU-Pro for DeepSeek-32B and 58.0% for QwQ-32B. Tree GNN gains averaged over tasks per model: +5.58, +5.72, +4.69, +3.89, +8.27 points.
limits: Tree is built by DeepSeek-V3 prompts, so it needs an LLM pass. GNN trained per setting.
agent_relevance: Structure beats length as a predictor, which supports a step-graph view over a token counter.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) LCoT2Tree: structural patterns of long chain-of-thought predict correctness
finding: Four error shapes found in trees of wrong answers: over-branching, step redundancy, direct reasoning that jumps many steps with little branching, and skipped thinking.
numbers: (A) over branching, excessive exploration or verification from one node; (B) step redundancy; (C) direct reasoning; (D) skipped thinking. Tree-based Best-of-N on LiveCodeBench v6 beat ORM-best and PRM-best baselines (Figure 5).
limits: Patterns come from GNN explanations on correlational data. Best-of-N test used hard items filtered by past errors, which can inflate gains.
agent_relevance: Over-branching is the wild-goose-chase shape. Too little branching is also a failure, so a detector needs a band, not a ceiling.

source: Feng et al. (2025) What characterizes effective reasoning? Revisiting length, review, and structure of CoT
finding: Within a question, longer chains and more review go with lower accuracy. The share of failed steps in a reasoning graph is the strongest predictor. Removing failed branches raises accuracy, so earlier mistakes bias later reasoning.
numbers: Ten reasoning models; HARP maths (300 questions, 50 per level 1 to 6) and GPQA-Diamond (198). 16 traces per question. Failed-Step Fraction selection gains roughly 5 to 13 points on AIME 2025 (64 samples). Branch editing: DeepSeek R1 original 20.89 vs reduced 29.42 (first branch), 9.72 vs 23.75 (last branch); GPT-oss 120B 28.05 vs 36.41 and 16.50 vs 27.33. 80 and 160 incorrect traces, 11,520 continuations.
quote: current models do not fully 'unsee' earlier mistakes when backtracking
limits: Read the HTML page through a summarising reader, not the full PDF text. Claude 3.7 on maths is an exception for review ratio. Qwen results on HARP excluded for suspected contamination. Failed steps are labelled by Claude 3.7.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G10: failed attempts left in context poison later steps. Strip failed branches or restate the problem fresh after a failure.

source: Kargupta et al. (2025) Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
finding: A 28-element taxonomy of cognitive processes applied to 192K model traces. Models under-use elements that correlate with success and default to forward chaining; successful traces on diagnosis scope the problem first.
numbers: 192,709 traces from 18 models; 54 human think-aloud traces; 1,598 arXiv papers. Logical coherence in 91% of traces (PPMI .091); knowledge alignment 20.2% (PPMI .234); spatial organisation 9.8% (PPMI .252); evaluation 53.5% (PPMI .031). Forward chaining probability 0.748 for common model traces. Guidance gain up to 66.7% on complex problems.
limits: Read only the first 100,000 of 243,635 characters of the HTML. PPMI is an association score. The 66.7% is the best case, not typical.
agent_relevance: An explicit scoping step at the start (our S1 and S2) may matter more than a big verify step.

source: Marjanovic et al. (2025) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM reasoning
finding: R1 traces follow four phases: problem definition, a long blooming cycle, reconstruction cycles, final decision. Rumination (repeating earlier ideas) rises with difficulty. Accuracy rises, peaks and falls with thought length.
numbers: 400 annotated examples (100 each: maths, context faithfulness, psycholinguistic stimuli, harmful QA). Rumination measured by 5-gram repetition plus lexical entropy. Max budget 32,000 tokens. AIME-24: 30 problems x 50 samples. GSM8K unconstrained average 1,388 tokens; budgets 64 to 1,024 cut output tokens by nearly half with little loss.
limits: Read the first 100,000 of about 400,000 characters. Rumination rate is independent of total processing time. The sweet spot is task and model specific.
agent_relevance: A phase view of R1 that fits the episode view. A 5-gram repeat rate is a cheap code-only stuck signal.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners
finding: Four behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) decide whether RL helps. Priming a weak model with the behaviours helps even when the primed solutions are wrong.
numbers: Countdown, PPO 250 steps. After RL, Qwen-2.5-3B reaches about 60% and Llama-3.2-3B about 30%. Priming on wrong solutions that show the behaviours matches priming on correct ones. Countdown RL transferred to MATH raised Qwen backtracking 0.15 to 0.59 and verification 0.02 to 0.29.
quote: the presence of reasoning behaviors, rather than correctness of answers, proves to be the critical factor
limits: Training based, Countdown only. Backward-chaining labeller agreement with humans is 0.40 to 0.55, so that label is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Behaviour presence matters more than a trace being correct, so do not read correctness from the episode mix alone.

source: Bogdan et al. (2025) Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
finding: Sentence-level counterfactual resampling finds a few anchor sentences. Plan-generation and uncertainty-management sentences matter most to the final answer. Active computation matters least by the counterfactual measure.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B on 20 MATH problems solved 25 to 75% of the time, 40 traces, mean 144.2 sentences and 4,208 tokens. 100 rollouts per sentence. Shares: active computation 32.7%, fact retrieval 20.1%, plan generation 15.5%, uncertainty management 14.0%, problem setup 2.4%, final answer 0.7%.
limits: Small problem set (20), one main model. Taxonomy is not Schoenfeld's but maps roughly: plan generation to Plan, uncertainty management to Monitor or Explore.
agent_relevance: Plan and uncertainty sentences steer the trace. This fits a design where code steers at the plan boundary.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking
finding: When a question is unsolvable because a premise is missing, reasoning models write 2 to 4 times longer answers and rarely abstain, though they notice the problem early. A clear wild-goose-chase case.
numbers: MiP-GSM8K 582 items, MiP-SVAMP 300. Non-reasoning models about 200 tokens on well-defined items. DeepSeek-R1 about 1,000 rising above 3,000 under missing premises. MiP-Formula abstain rates: GPT-o1 78.0%, GPT-4o 70.0%, DeepSeek-R1 6.0%, QwQ-32B 0.0%; QwQ averages 7,937 tokens. Suspicion shown in 83.3 to 100% of traces, first at step index 1.16 to 1.42.
limits: Some dataset counts were garbled in the page readout. Read through a summarising reader, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Models know early they are stuck but do not stop. A code rule that stops on a repeated 'this seems unsolvable' note is justified by this.

source: Synthesis across Li 2025, ThinkARM, Wang 2025, Feng 2025, Jiang 2025
finding: Three families of stuck signal appear in the evidence: (1) episode shape (high Explore share, Explore not routed to Monitor or Analyze), (2) switching (many thoughts, none deepened), (3) failed-step share. None has been validated online against an intervention. All are correlations on finished traces.
numbers: Strongest numbers: Explore ratio coefficient -0.54 and Exp-to-Mon +0.41 (ThinkARM); over 70% of wrong answers held a correct thought (Wang); failed-branch removal +8 to +14 points (Feng).
limits: No paper tests an online detector that stops or redirects a model mid-generation, and none separates difficulty from error in the correlations. Annotator noise (about 86% agreement on gold) adds to this.
agent_relevance: Test any online detector in our harness first: detector-triggered restarts vs plain at equal tokens (G7).
